# Institutional toolkit: results

<!-- Generated by `python -m dpc.cli institutional` from reports/institutional/summary.json. Do not edit. -->

Not pre-registered. These are tools with tests (`tests/test_institutional.py`), applied once to public data (Kenneth French's library and FRED). Every number below comes from `summary.json`.

## 1. Active management against the market: factor risk model, Black-Litterman, a tracking-error budget

Long-only across the 30 industries, benchmark the cap-weighted market, decided monthly with past data only, 1970-01 to 2026-09 (681 months), net of 10 bps per unit traded.

| Tracking-error budget | Active return a year | Newey-West t | Realised tracking error | Information ratio | Bias statistic | Turnover a year |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1% | 0.54% | 3.24 | 1.27% | 0.42 | 1.27 | 119% |
| 2% | 1.08% | 3.35 | 2.50% | 0.43 | 1.25 | 219% |
| 4% | 1.88% | 2.92 | 4.76% | 0.39 | 1.20 | 385% |

**Is the risk model right?** The bias statistic is the standard deviation of active return divided by the model's forecast of tracking error; 1 is a perfect forecast, and with 681 months the band is 0.95 to 1.05. Three risk models, same budget (2%):

| Risk model | Bias statistic | Realised tracking error | Information ratio | Verdict |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Factor model (market, size, value) + specific | 1.25 | 2.50% | 0.43 | risk under-forecast |
| Sample covariance, Ledoit-Wolf shrinkage | 1.11 | 2.22% | 0.40 | risk under-forecast |
| Sample covariance | 1.15 | 2.30% | 0.40 | risk under-forecast |

A three-factor model treats what is left after market, size and value as unrelated across industries; industries in the same sector are not, so the model under-forecasts the risk of bets that lean on a sector. That is the reason commercial models carry industry factors.

**Where the active risk sits (2026-09).** 57% of the active variance comes from the factors and 43% is specific. Largest contributors:

| Industry | Active weight | Share of active risk |
|---|---:|---:|
| BusEq | 4.71% | 43.4% |
| Steel | 2.37% | 33.1% |
| ElcEq | 1.92% | 24.2% |
| FabPr | 2.19% | 22.4% |
| Mines | 1.65% | 14.9% |
| Autos | -1.27% | -10.1% |
| Trans | 1.06% | 7.6% |
| Rtail | -1.03% | -6.3% |

**Brinson-Fachler attribution, 2% budget, gross of costs, sectors grouped from the 30 industries.** Average effect per year over 1970-01 to 2026-09: allocation 0.93%, selection 0.43%, interaction -0.06%. Linked over the last ten years (2016-10 to 2026-09, Carino): 414.0% against 310.2%, active 103.7%, split 94.7% allocation, 5.2% selection, 3.9% interaction. The same attribution in SQL (DuckDB) agrees with pandas to 4e-15.

| Sector | Allocation a year | Selection a year | Interaction a year | Total a year | Last 10 years, linked |

**Read with care.** The view is momentum because the wealth study (this repository) had already found a momentum tilt to be the strongest classical rule over the same history. The view was chosen knowing that, so a t-statistic here is not independent evidence of an edge; what this section demonstrates is the machinery and the risk-model check.


## 2. The yield curve: Nelson-Siegel-Svensson, principal components, key-rate durations

US Treasury constant-maturity yields (FRED), every month-end since 1990 (443 curves). Median fit error 3.0 bp (95th percentile 6.5 bp). Monthly changes of the fitted 1- to 30-year curve, 442 months: level explains 90.5%, slope 6.9%, curvature 1.2%; together 98.6%.

## 3. The pension promise with mortality: solvency and going-concern

A closed cohort (actives 30 to 60, retirees 65 to 95), pensions indexed at 2% a year, Gompertz-Makeham mortality (the textbook Standard Ultimate Survival Model; life expectancy at 65: 22.2 years). Valued on the Treasury curve of 2026-11.

| Basis | Value | Duration |
|---|---:|---:|
| Solvency (zero curve) | 2,784 | 16.4 |
| Going concern, 6% assumed return | 2,481 | 14.4 |
| Going concern, 5% assumed return | 2,885 | |

Key-rate durations: 2y 0.26, 5y 0.88, 10y 2.86, 20y 4.55, 30y 7.82 (they add up to the solvency duration). Death rates 20% lower at every age (life expectancy at 65: 23.9) raise the liability by 6.8%.

## 4. LDI with a swap overlay: funding risk against liquidity risk

A plan 95% funded: 30% in long bonds, 5% cash, 65% return-seeking; receive-fixed swaps make up the hedge.

| Hedge ratio | Leverage | Funded ratio, yields −1 pt | yields +1 pt | +1 pt and equities −20% | Margin call, +1 pt | Largest rise the collateral meets |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 28% (bonds only) | 1.00x | -10.5 pts | +11.4 pts | -3.2 pts | 0.0 | no swaps |
| 50% | 1.25x | -7.4 pts | +7.1 pts | -7.4 pts | 3.6 | 403 bp |
| 75% | 1.54x | -3.9 pts | +2.3 pts | -12.2 pts | 7.7 | 267 bp |
| 100% | 1.83x | -0.4 pts | -2.5 pts | -17.1 pts | 11.8 | 200 bp |

The worst rises in the US 30-year yield since 1977: 50 bp in a day (1980-02-19), 95 bp in a week (1980-02-21), 208 bp in a month (1980-02-21); since 2000: 50 bp in a week (2009-01-26), 99 bp in a month (2009-01-29). Hedging steadies the funded ratio; it is the swaps' cash calls, not the funding position, that a fast rise tests. A plan below full funding that hedges all of its liability's DV01 is over-hedged in funded-ratio terms (its assets are smaller than what it hedges), which is why the 100% row loses when yields rise.

## 5. Currency: hedging US equities for a Canadian investor

US stock market in Canadian dollars, 1971-02 to 2026-09 (668 months). The minimum-variance hedge ratio is **0.00** (no hedge at all); over rolling 10-year windows it ranged from -0.67 to 0.58 (latest -0.41). In the 24 worst months for US stocks the US dollar rose 2.4% on average against the Canadian dollar.

| Hedge ratio | Volatility a year | Worst month | Worst fall |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 0.00 | 14.3% | -22.2% | -48.7% |
| 0.50 | 14.7% | -22.4% | -46.8% |
| 1.00 | 15.8% | -22.7% | -52.4% |

## 6. Private assets: fund cash flows, pacing, the denominator effect, desmoothing

**One fund (Takahashi-Alexander, illustrative buyout parameters).** 100% of the commitment is ever called; the cumulative net cash flow bottoms at -80% of commitment (the J-curve) and turns positive in year 8; TVPI 1.71x, IRR 11.0%.

**A programme.** To hold 25% in private assets while paying out 2% of assets a year in net benefits, the plan commits 5.0% of its assets every year, and needs 8 years to reach 90% of the target. A 30% fall in public markets in year 25 lifts the private share from 25.0% to 33.4% overnight: the denominator effect. A rule that commits less while over target cuts new commitments to 0.0% of assets in the years right after the crash, the step a plan takes to get back to target (and the vintages it then skips).

**Desmoothing.** Quarterly returns of a series with known volatility (the construction industry's quarterly returns, a stand-in with known volatility) smoothed as an appraisal would (phi = 0.6): reported volatility 7.0% a quarter against a true 14.9%; Geltner's correction (estimated phi 0.53) gives 12.6%. Correlation with the stock market: true 0.93, smoothed 0.76, desmoothed 0.93.


## 7. Market risk: does a 99% VaR forecast hold up?

US stock market, monthly total return (Kenneth French), one-month 99% VaR forecast each month from the previous 120 months, 1936-07 to 2026-09. A sound model is exceeded in 1% of months (Kupiec) and its exceptions do not cluster (Christoffersen); a test is passed when p > 0.05.

| Model | Average VaR | Exceptions (expected) | Kupiec p | Back-to-back exceptions | Christoffersen p |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Historical simulation | 10.9% | 23 (10.8) | 0.001 | 3 | 0.011 |
| Normal, window mean and volatility | 10.2% | 24 (10.8) | 0.001 | 3 | 0.014 |
| Normal, EWMA volatility (lambda 0.97) | 10.9% | 17 (10.8) | 0.082 | 1 | 0.265 |

Average historical expected shortfall (the mean loss beyond VaR, the Basel III measure): 13.3%; the average loss in the months that did exceed VaR: 11.2%.

## Limits

- 30 industries are not stocks: the active study has 30 assets and one view; its information ratio is not a claim about a stock picker.
- The risk model has three public factors; commercial models have dozens. The bias statistic shows what that costs.
- The mortality table is a textbook Gompertz-Makeham model, not CPM2014; the plan is illustrative, not a real plan's membership.
- LDI: parallel shifts, one swap tenor, no repo, no rebalancing during the shock.
- FX: the hedge ignores the interest-rate differential (carry), which changes returns, not this variance.
- Private-fund parameters are illustrative, not fitted to managers' cash flows.
